newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Swedish alcohol monopoly challenged in EU court.
newsitem.headline: Swedish alcohol monopoly challenged in EU court.

text.p: The Swedish state alcohol monopoly is being challenged in the European Court of Justice in a controversial case which could force the country to change its stringent liquor laws.
The district court of the Swedish town of Landskrona has asked the EU Court for a preliminary ruling on whether the monopoly over retail liquor sales is compatible with European Union law.

The oral hearing on the case, which will see interventions from the Swedish, Finnish and Norwegian governments as well as by the European Commission, takes place on Tuesday but a verdict is not expected until the first half of next year.
The case involves an action brought by the Landskrona public prosecutor against grocer Harry Franzen for breaking the monopoly of the state-owned Systembolaget over sales of wine and spirits.
"If the EU court finds that the monopoly contravenes EU law then it is clear that we can't keep our Systembolaget," Landskrona district court judge Stellan Fors told the Swedish news agency TT.
Determined to see if Sweden's stringent alcohol legislation complied with EU rules, Franzen started selling wine in his shop in 1994.

Franzen sold one-litre sealed packs of white and red French, Italian and Spanish wine for 65 crowns ($9.80) each but, as expected, he was soon interrupted by plain-clothes policemen who ordered him to stop.
"Finally, this has taken a long time. The first time I sold wine was on January 1, 1994," Franzen told TT.
The Landskrona court has asked the EU Court whether the Swedish alcohol monopoly is compatible with articles 30 and 37 in the Treaty of Rome.
Article 30 bans quantitative restrictions on imports.

Article 37 says that member states "shall progressively adjust any state monopolies of a commercial character so as to ensure that when the transitional period ended no discrimination regarding the conditions under which goods are procured and marketed exists between nationals of member states".
When Sweden became an EU member in 1995, the Commission accepted its century-old retail monopoly as long as it did not discriminate against imports from other EU states.

The monopoly's survival was a victory for the government and influential temperance movements who argue the public must be protected from "the dangers of higher alcohol consumption" such as higher mortality from cirrhosis of the liver.
But Franzen argues that small shopkeepers in communities like his, the southern Swedish village of Rostanga, population 1,000, feel the rules are out of date.
Franzen says that allowing thousands of small shops to sell wine alongside the weak beer currently permitted on their shelves would not damage national health.
Finland and Norway, which also have state alcohol monopolies, are expected to support Sweden's position.
